The One Number That Earns Its Keep

A case-style treatment of the North Star metric, for practitioners who already know the definition.

1. Two Rooms, Two Weeks Apart

On the morning of 11 August 2026, Devika Raghunath opened the FY27 planning review at Lohit Coldchain Systems in Pune with a slide showing three arrows pointing in three directions. Lohit sold battery-powered temperature loggers that ride inside refrigerated consignments — vaccines, insulin, semen straws, paneer — paired with a monitoring console that alerts a distributor when a consignment drifts out of its contracted band. FY26 revenue was ₹214 crore — ₹86 crore of one-time hardware, ₹128 crore of subscription — across 54,300 active devices at 1,180 customer sites.

The three arrows were the problem. The hardware unit in Coimbatore was measured on units shipped, and shipped 4,900 a month. The platform team in Hyderabad was measured on subscription ARR. Field operations in Kolkata was measured on installation SLA. Each had hit its number for six consecutive quarters while net revenue retention fell from 104 per cent to 95. In June a national pharma distributor put Lohit on notice after fourteen excursion alerts sat unacknowledged for an average of nine hours; the consignments were fine, but nobody could prove it, which for a customer operating under CDSCO cold-chain expectations is the same thing. The board's instruction was blunt: bring back one number for FY27 that all three cities can be held to.

Fifteen days later, Sohini Barua faced the mirror-image problem at Jhalar Live, a Bengaluru live-commerce marketplace where handloom sellers in Varanasi, Bhagalpur and Surat run streams for tier-two buyers. The quarter had been spectacular by the number the Series C investors cared about: gross merchandise value up 34 per cent to ₹212 crore. Her seller-operations head in Varanasi sent a one-line message the night before the board call: we are losing the weavers who actually show up. Returns had risen from 22 to 31 per cent. The count of sellers clearing ₹50,000 a month had fallen from 1,860 to 1,410 even as GMV rose by half. Sohini had to decide whether to accept GMV as the company's North Star, which would make the fundraise easier and the next four quarters worse.

2. What the Idea Actually Claims, and Who Disputes It

Definition. A North Star metric is a single quantitative expression of the value customers receive from a product, chosen such that sustained movement in it causally precedes movement in the firm's long-run economics, and stated at a granularity that lets every team derive an input they own.

Three clauses do the work, and each is contested. Value customers receive rules out revenue, bookings and gross margin, which are the firm's take, not the customer's gain. Causally precedes rules out both vanity counts that correlate with nothing and lagging outcomes that correlate with everything after the fact. Lets every team derive an input they own is the clause practitioners skip, and the one that makes a North Star an operating instrument rather than a poster.

The lineage runs through four traditions that did not know they were building the same thing. Andrew Grove's High Output Management (1983) insisted that output measures be paired with controllable input measures, because managers can only act on inputs. Amazon's working-backwards discipline made that operational: a small set of controllable input metrics argued about in writing, with outputs treated as consequences rather than goals. Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics (2013) supplied the reductive move — one metric at a time, deliberately crude, changing by stage. Sean Ellis and the growth practitioners supplied the customer-value anchor, the activation moment after which retention visibly changes. Amplitude's North Star Playbook (2018), with John Cutler, fused these into the form most teams now use: one metric plus an explicit input tree.

Against this sits the older sceptical tradition. Goodhart's observation, in Marilyn Strathern's restatement, is that a measure which becomes a target ceases to be a good measure; Campbell said the same of social indicators; Jerry Muller's The Tyranny of Metrics (2018) catalogues the institutional damage. The sceptics do not argue for measuring nothing. They argue that the coordination benefit of a single number is bought with a distortion cost that grows with the number's salience in compensation.

What each school would and would not sign is worth stating precisely, because the disagreements are not stylistic.

3. The Mechanics, Worked Rather Than Named

Expert practice has seven steps. The first three are taught everywhere; the last four are where competent teams quietly stop.

Step one: state the value exchange in one sentence. For Lohit: distributors get evidence that a consignment stayed in band and that anyone who needed to act did; Lohit gets subscription revenue that renews because that evidence has regulatory and insurance value. Note the exclusion — the device is not the value, which is why shipments were never a candidate.

Step two: enumerate every metric the event stream can actually produce, not the ones you wish it produced. Lohit's telemetry could yield shipments, active devices, consignments monitored, consignment-hours, hours in band, hours in band with an acknowledged excursion trail, and a modelled rupee value of spoilage prevented.

Step three: test each candidate against a downstream outcome out of sample. Lohit's data team in Hyderabad computed each candidate at month one of the contract year for all 1,180 sites and ranked them against realised twelve-month net revenue retention, fitting on FY25 sites and scoring FY26 ones. That split matters: in sample, every candidate looks respectable.

Step seven: set the review cadence and the restatement rule. Protected hours stay provisional for fourteen days while excursion dispositions settle, so Lohit's Monday review reads the lagged number as final and the current fortnight as provisional. Teams that refuse to restate end up optimising the truncated early version of their own metric.

4. The Conditions, Stated So They Can Fail

The claim that a business should have a North Star is not universal. It holds when five conditions hold, each of which can be checked and can be false.

C1 — the value delivered can be counted in one unit without hiding mix. Lohit passes: an hour in band is an hour in band, whether the cargo is insulin or paneer. Jhalar fails: a ₹700 cotton sari and a ₹70,000 Banarasi sari are not the same value event, to the buyer or the weaver. Jhalar must value-weight the metric or accept that it counts transactions, not value.

C2 — the metric can be read faster than decisions are made. Lohit passes with a two-week settle. Jhalar passes only conditionally: its ten-day return window means any weekly reading is an estimate that will be revised downward, and the size of that revision is exactly the thing management most needs to watch.

C3 — a decision inside one planning cycle can move it. Both pass. Modelled spoilage prevented fails, which is why it sits below the North Star as a validation measure, not above it as a goal.

C4 — either one customer's value dominates, or the sides' interests are aligned under the chosen definition. Lohit passes; the distributor is the only customer. Jhalar fails under GMV and passes under a value-weighted kept-purchase metric, because a kept purchase is good for the buyer and good for the weaver simultaneously, while a discounted, returned purchase is good for neither and excellent for GMV.

C5 — the organisation can be cut so each input has exactly one owner. Lohit passes, barely, once hours per consignment is declared unowned. Firms that fail C5 usually discover it only after adoption, when two teams claim the same input and neither is accountable for it.

The idea is actively misleading in four situations. When a firm is deliberately buying a market at negative unit economics, a customer-value metric looks magnificent while the business dies; the honest North Star is then a unit-economic one, and saying so is the point. When value events are rare and lumpy — claims settlement, an annual tax filing — the metric has no usable frequency and a proxy must be substituted knowingly. When a regulator defines value, as with payment-system uptime norms or telecom quality-of-service standards, thresholds dominate and a smooth metric hides threshold risk. And during a platform shift the old metric measures the old product; retaining it is how incumbents optimise their way out of a market.

5. Edge Cases and Organisational Seams

Two-sided. Jhalar's arithmetic is the canonical demonstration. Over four quarters GMV rose 52 per cent, ₹140 crore to ₹212 crore. Kept GMV — delivered, past the return window, unrefunded — rose 13 per cent, ₹109 crore to ₹123 crore, as returns climbed from 22 to 31 per cent under a coupon-funded push. Meanwhile the supply side, where a live-commerce marketplace's inventory of trust sits, contracted: sellers clearing ₹50,000 a month fell 24 per cent. Three numbers, one business, one of them in the investor deck.

Hardware plus software. Lohit's seam is structural, not cultural. The hardware P&L books revenue on shipment; the SaaS P&L books it over a subscription that renews only if devices are used. A device in a distributor's store cupboard is a win for one unit and a slow loss for the other. The North Star resolves this by construction: shipments enter the tree only through devices per site, and only devices that report. Mature hardware firms keep both numbers and are explicit that one is a revenue-recognition number, not a value number; those that pretend otherwise end up with channel stuffing dressed as growth.

Multi-product. When a firm sells unrelated value to unrelated buyers, one North Star is a category error, and the usual fix — a weighted composite — produces a number whose movements nobody can interpret. What large firms actually do, whatever the annual report says, is run a North Star per business unit and hold one genuinely shared metric above them, usually accounts using two or more products in a period. That is not the company's North Star; it is the number that justifies the company existing as one company rather than three.

Regulated. In payments, lending and health the binding constraint is a threshold, not a mean. A product whose North Star is successful transactions can run a fine average while breaching downtime norms in a way that draws supervisory attention. What works is a North Star plus a small set of hard gates that are never traded off, only reported.

AI-native. This case breaks the older playbooks. Lipi Docs, a contract-review product in Gurugram, shipped a model upgrade in March 2026. Average agent turns per contract fell from 9.4 to 3.1, sessions per user fell 41 per cent, time in product fell by a third: every engagement metric collapsed. Contracts cleared per lawyer-day rose from 6.2 to 14.8, and renewal intent rose with it. A firm with an engagement North Star would have read the best quarter in its history as the worst. For AI products the metric must be denominated in completed customer outcomes, because the product's whole purpose is to cut the interaction needed to reach them.

The seams. Three predictably break a good metric. Sales compensation, which pays on bookings and wins any conflict with a usage metric unless the plan changes, which it usually does not. The FP&A model, which forecasts in a taxonomy that does not map to the tree, so the two drift and the board reverts to the finance view. And the planning calendar: definitions are revised in the first quarter, targets set from the old definition, and the year spent comparing two different numbers.

6. What Separates the Expert

The unit carries the argument. Most disputes that look like disagreements about which metric to pick are disagreements about its unit. Hours, counts, rupees and users behave differently under mix shift. The tell is a team arguing for weeks about candidate metrics that are all the same quantity in different clothing; an expert redirects the conversation to what a single unit of delivered value physically is, and the metric usually falls out in an hour.

Ratios hide composition. A per-user North Star can improve for the worst possible reason: light users churned. The tell is the ratio rising while the numerator is flat and the denominator is shrinking. The discipline is to publish magnitude and ratio side by side and to require that a claimed improvement in the ratio be visible within a fixed cohort, not across the changing population.

In-sample validation is nearly free and nearly worthless. Any metric computed from the same event stream as revenue will correlate with it, especially if the two share a denominator such as account count. The tell is a correlation above 0.8 obtained in an afternoon. Experts fit on one period, score on a later one, and read the drop between them as information about the metric rather than noise.

Guardrails must be structurally independent. A counter-metric that the same action improves is decoration. Lohit's guardrail — disputed excursion reports per ten thousand protected hours — works because the only way to inflate protected hours artificially, loosening the verification bar, drives disputes up. The tell of a fake guardrail is that it has never once been the reason a launch was stopped.

The quality bar is most of the metric. Where the threshold sits — thirty minutes rather than four hours, a kept order rather than a placed one — usually matters more than which family of metric was chosen. The tell is a redefinition proposal that makes the number larger and is justified on grounds of data availability. Experts ask what the looser definition does to out-of-sample predictive power before asking what it does to the chart.

Two owners means none. An input claimed by two teams will be optimised by neither when it is hard and by both when it is easy. The tell is a tree where one box has a slash in its owner field. The correct move is either to split the input until each piece has one owner or to declare it unowned context, as Lohit did with hours per consignment.

Late-arriving data forces restatement. Returns, refunds, disputes and churn settle after the fact, so this week's number is an estimate. Teams that never restate optimise the truncated early reading, which favours actions that book value fast. The tell is a metric never revised downward after publication in a business where refunds exist.

The metric is a coordination device first. How many teams can state, unprompted, the input they own predicts whether a North Star will work better than its correlation coefficient does. The tell is a technically excellent metric that appears only in the monthly business review. An expert trades several points of predictive power for a definition a field engineer in Kolkata can explain without a slide.

7. How It Differs by Product Type and Stage

In consumer products the North Star is usually a frequency or depth measure of the core action, and the hard part is the quality bar separating engagement from value. In B2B the honest version is narrower than the flattering one: not accounts logging in, but accounts whose contracted workflow actually runs through the product weekly, since a tool bought to replace a process is often used for one trivial corner of it. In enterprise the buyer, the administrator and the user hold three different notions of value; the usual resolution is a usage metric with a buyer-visible outcome guardrail.

Platforms and marketplaces must encode both sides or pair the metric with an explicit supply floor, as Jhalar shows. Hardware faces the shipment-versus-use seam, and consumer packaged goods genuinely break the frame: with no telemetry, the closest constructs are velocity per outlet, weighted distribution and repeat rate, and calling one of them a North Star overstates what the data supports. AI products invert the engagement logic entirely. Across stages the difference is real: a pre-product-market-fit team should take a crude proxy quickly, since any shared number beats a correct one arriving late, while a scaled firm's constraint is coordination rather than measurement and its tree matters more than its top number.

8. Three Worked Cases, One of Them a Failure

Lohit. The recovery in Figure 1's Panel B came from a single input. Compliant-and-verified share rose from 72 to 84 per cent; holding the other four factors constant, that alone would have lifted protected hours by 16.7 per cent. It moved because alert routing was rebuilt to reach the person on shift rather than the account owner — a decision that would not have been funded under any of the three previous metrics.

Jhalar. Recomputed under a kept-GMV definition, a 52 per cent growth story became a 13 per cent one — and roughly ₹89 crore of Q4 GMV turned out to be goods that came back, cost a weaver a wasted production slot, and cost Jhalar about ₹6.2 crore in reverse logistics.

Lavangi Foods, where it failed. The Jaipur spice and ready-mix brand adopted orders per month as its North Star in FY24 on the advice that a simple metric beats a clever one. It was simple, actionable, leading, and wrong.

The metric was not gamed in any dishonest sense — it was satisfied exactly as written, by people doing their jobs well. The failure was the validation step nobody ran: ranking FY23 cohorts by first-month orders against twelve-month contribution would have shown the correlation to be visibly weak.

The recovery is instructive because it was mostly not analytical. The new metric — households placing a second or later full-price order in a rolling ninety days — took a fortnight to choose, then fell 23 per cent in its first quarter as coupon traffic was cut, and the founder spent two board meetings defending a chart going down. What made it stick came four months later, when the growth team's variable pay moved off order volume. Until then the new number was reported and the old one optimised.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Whether one number should ever override functional metrics. The coordination camp argues that the entire value of a North Star is its authority in a tie, and that a metric which never overrides anything is a slogan. The growth-model camp argues that this authority is precisely what invites Goodhart distortion, and that the tree, reviewed as a system, coordinates perfectly well without a single arbiter. The evidence is mixed because the outcome depends on compensation design, which studies rarely control for. The coordination camp would be wrong if firms with published North Stars showed no faster resolution of cross-team disputes than firms with metric trees alone.

Whether the metric should be validated statistically or chosen strategically. The validation camp points to Lavangi, where a defensible-sounding metric destroyed contribution and a twenty-minute cohort analysis would have caught it. The strategy camp answers that the metric's job is to state what the firm intends to become, that historical correlation is estimated on the product you are trying to stop building, and that a firm pivoting toward AI-assisted outcomes finds every historical correlation pointing backwards. Lipi Docs is their evidence. They would be wrong if narrative-chosen metrics predicted outcomes about as badly as sceptics assume — which nobody has tested.

Whether two-sided businesses can have one. One camp holds that a sufficiently well-defined single metric, like kept and value-weighted purchases, is simultaneously good for both sides and that two metrics simply defer the trade-off. The other holds that supply and demand health genuinely diverge in the short run and that a supply floor must be a separate, hard commitment rather than a term inside a composite. This one is unresolved in practice; mature marketplaces mostly run a demand-side North Star and a supply-side floor and describe it as one metric in public.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a candidate metric. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a unit of value, an identity that decomposes it, a named owner per factor, and a list of what the metric will not catch. They can say what would make them abandon it, and they check that condition annually rather than waiting for it to become obvious. In a disagreement they ask what unit the proposals are counting, not which correlates better. They treat the compensation plan as part of the measurement system, because it is. And they are comfortable presenting a number going down, because the first quarter after an honest redefinition almost always looks worse than the dishonest quarter before it.

12. What Each Protagonist Decided

Devika took protected consignment-hours to the FY27 charter with the five-factor tree, one owner per factor, hours per consignment declared unowned, and the disputed-report guardrail read in the same Monday meeting rather than a separate quality review. She kept modelled spoilage prevented as a twice-yearly validation measure below the North Star, and committed to re-estimating the renewal elasticity each October. The hardware shipment target survived, reframed as a factor inside the tree rather than a competing goal.

Sohini declined GMV. Jhalar's FY27 North Star became kept purchase value per active buyer per quarter, with a supply floor — sellers clearing ₹50,000 a month — stated as a hard commitment rather than folded into a composite, on the view that the two genuinely diverge and that hiding the trade-off inside one number only moves the argument somewhere less visible. She expected reported growth to fall from 52 per cent to roughly 13, and briefed the investors before the definition changed, not after.

For discussion: (1) Lohit's guardrail and North Star are both computed by the same platform team in Hyderabad — is that independence enough, and what would you change? (2) Sohini chose two numbers where the orthodoxy prescribes one; under what conditions would a single value-weighted metric have served Jhalar better, and how would you test it before committing? (3) Lavangi's recovery required changing variable pay. If a firm cannot change compensation this year, is adopting a new North Star worth doing at all, or does it simply add a reported number to an unchanged system of incentives?

13. Going Deeper

  • Product vision and mission — the vision reduced to a number; a mismatch here is fatal.
  • OKRs and goal setting — turning the tree's inputs into commitments.
  • Attention, transaction, productivity games — the game you play picks the metric family.
  • Breadth × depth × frequency — the standard identity for usage products.
  • One Metric That Matters — the stage-varying sibling, and where it diverges.
  • B2B product metrics — workflow penetration beats seat counts.
  • Hardware and connected-product metrics — the shipment-versus-use seam in full.
  • CPG metrics: velocity, distribution, share — when there is no telemetry at all.
  • The value metric — pricing's version of the same question.
  • Marketplace metrics — liquidity, match rate, and supply floors.
  • Developer product metrics — adoption through code, not sessions.
  • Product metrics for AI features — outcome denomination when usage falls.

  • GAME framework — goal to metric when the unit is unclear.
  • Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — where each input sits.
  • Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — Section 6's composition traps.
  • Input vs output; leading vs lagging — Figure 3's axes, formally.
  • Guardrail metrics — building a counter-metric that can bind.
  • Metric ownership and cadence — whether any of this survives contact.

The One Number: North Star Metrics

A working explainer

1. A Number for the Board

On the morning of 14 September 2026, Ritika Deshpande walked into the Bengaluru boardroom of Manzil Career Cloud with a slide she was not proud of. Manzil ran a skilling app for young people preparing for entry-level jobs in retail, warehousing, and logistics — short courses, a proctored assessment, and a certificate that hiring partners had agreed to treat as a screening signal. Monthly active users had sat at 2.1 million for two straight quarters. Course starts were healthy, 340,000 a month. But renewal into the paid Career Plus plan, which funded the assessment infrastructure and the content team in Hyderabad, had slipped from 34 percent to 27 percent, and two of Manzil's four hiring partners had quietly reduced intake, citing inconsistent quality among candidates hired off the platform.

The chairperson did not want a dashboard. She wanted one number. "Every team here — Pune engineering, Hyderabad content, Gurugram partnerships — is already optimising something," she said. "Tell us the one number that, if it moves the right way, tells us the whole company is getting healthier. Put it in the FY27 charter." Ritika had three weeks. A number that was easy to move but meaningless — active users — would let the company hit target while renewal kept sliding and hiring partners kept walking away. A number too far downstream — placements six months out — meant no team could act on it fast enough to matter this year. Whatever she picked would be the thing three cities argued about for the next twelve months.

Figure 1. Activity looked stable while the metric tied to revenue and to hiring-partner trust eroded — the exact pattern that makes boards ask for one number instead of many.

2. What a North Star Metric Is

A North Star metric is the single quantitative measure of the value a product delivers to its customers, chosen specifically because sustained movement in that number reliably predicts the long-run financial health of the business. It is not a KPI in the ordinary sense — a company tracks dozens of KPIs — and it is not the same as revenue, which is an outcome of many things, including price changes and sales headcount, that have nothing to do with whether the product itself is getting better. The North Star sits between the two: closer to the customer than revenue, but chosen precisely because it is not merely popular or easy to measure.

The term crystallised in the growth and product-analytics community between roughly 2013 and 2018. Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz, in Lean Analytics (2013), argued that at any stage a company should track "One Metric That Matters" rather than a wall of dashboards, because a single focal number forces hard prioritisation. Sean Ellis and the growth-hacking practitioners who followed tied this metric to the moment a user first experiences the product's core value — the "aha moment." By 2018 the analytics company Amplitude had formalised the practice as the "North Star Playbook," a repeatable method for deriving the metric and decomposing it into inputs. Manzil's version did not need inventing from scratch; it needed applying correctly to a business selling two different things to two different audiences: a learning experience to job-seekers, a hiring signal to employers.

The sentence Ritika could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "Our North Star is the one number that only moves when a learner has genuinely gotten better at something and an employer can trust that fact — everything else on our dashboard is either an input to that number or a consequence of it."

3. How It Is Actually Derived

The method has six steps, and the last two are the ones most teams skip. First, state the value exchange in one sentence: what the customer gets, and what the business gets back. For Manzil: learners get a certified, employer-recognised skill; Manzil gets a share of the wage lift that certification enables, collected as subscription revenue and placement fees. Second, list every candidate the event data can actually produce — app opens, enrollments, module completions, assessment attempts and passes, certificates issued, employer-verified placements. Third — the step most teams shorten into a guess — test each candidate against a downstream outcome using cohort data, not intuition: does this number, measured in month one, predict retention or revenue in month three or four?

Fourth, check three properties together, since a metric can fail on any one even after passing the correlation test: is it leading rather than merely confirming what already happened; is it actionable by a product or content change this sprint; and is it resistant to gaming, meaning a team cannot inflate it by lowering quality. Fifth — left implicit most often — decompose the metric into an input tree: the sub-metrics that combine to produce it, each with a natural owner. Sixth, give each input an owner, a review cadence, and the specific decision it informs; a metric nobody reviews weekly quietly becomes decoration.

4. Working the Numbers

The arithmetic told a clear story. The 28.4 percent of learners who reached a verified completion produced 8,662 of the cohort's 13,579 total renewals — 64 percent of all renewal revenue from under a third of the users. Mere enrollment barely moved the needle: 42.6 percent of the cohort, only 30 percent of the renewals. That gap, not a hunch, told Ritika that "Verified Skill Completions" was a far better North Star candidate than "Monthly Active Users" or "Course Enrollments," the two numbers the board had been reading for two years.

Now run the second pass, changing one input: a metric's usefulness depends entirely on where its quality bar sits. Suppose the pass threshold dropped from 70 percent to simply "attempted." The qualifying group grows to roughly 19,000 — a bigger, more flattering number — but its blended 90-day renewal rate falls to about 38 percent, diluted by learners who attempted and failed. Total renewals from this redefined group come to roughly 7,220, fewer than the 8,662 from the smaller, stricter group. A metric that looks larger and grows faster can quietly become a worse predictor of the outcome it exists to track; the quality bar is not a technicality, it is most of the metric's value.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Sit With

A North Star is not a KPI dashboard

Boards and product teams routinely conflate "the metric we watch most" with "the North Star." The exercise is subtraction: one number that earns the right to override the other twenty when they disagree, not one more tile added to the wall.

Correlation is not causation

Verified Skill Completions correlated strongly with renewal, but that alone does not prove completing a module causes renewal — more motivated learners might simply do both. The rigorous next step is an experiment: does nudging borderline learners toward completion actually raise renewal, or does the correlation just reflect a trait the metric happens to capture?

Leading versus lagging is not optional

Employer-verified placements were, in principle, an even better predictor of long-run value — but placements arrive months after the decisions that influenced them, and by the time the count moves, the product team has shipped something else entirely. A North Star that cannot be moved and observed within a quarter fails the team meant to act on it.

It can be gamed if the definition is loose

Section 4's second pass is the general case: any metric a team is measured on will eventually be optimised toward its literal definition rather than its intent. The defence is a paired guardrail — for Manzil, complaints per hundred completions — that a team cannot improve by cutting corners on the North Star itself.

One North Star, but which side of a two-sided business?

Manzil sells to learners and employers at once. A metric that maximises learner-side activity can work against employer-side trust if it is not anchored to verified quality. "Verified" completions, rather than raw ones, was Manzil's way of serving both sides with a single number — though a genuine marketplace sometimes still needs an explicit tie-breaker for when the two sides' interests diverge.

It changes as the business model changes

Had Manzil's revenue shifted mostly to employer placement fees, the North Star would need to shift toward the employer's definition of value — verified, timely, low-attrition placements — even where that made it harder for the product team to move directly.

It cannot tell you what to build

A North Star tells a company whether it is heading the right way; it does not tell an engineer in Pune which of three features to ship this sprint. That translation is the job of the owned input tree in Figure 3 — the North Star sets the destination, not the itinerary.

It is a stage decision, not a permanent one

The right North Star for a four-person team validating an idea (often something crude, like "did anyone return tomorrow") is deliberately simpler than for a two-hundred-person company with paying enterprise customers, and revisiting it on a fixed cadence — Manzil chose annually — keeps it from calcifying into a number nobody remembers the reasoning behind.

6. Consumer, B2B, and Marketplace Differences

In a pure consumer product, the North Star typically approximates a single user's engaged time or frequency with the core action — the "aha" moment repeated. In B2B software the honest version is narrower and less flattering: not logins, but the number of accounts whose core workflow actually runs through the product weekly, since login counts can stay high while the product is used for one trivial task and ignored for the workflow it was bought to replace. In a marketplace like Manzil, the metric usually has to encode both sides — Uber's early North Star combined completed trips with driver availability, because trips alone could hide a supply shortage building underneath. Manzil's "verified completions" is the same compromise: a learner-side action defined strictly enough to double as the employer-side trust signal.

Stage matters as much as model. An early-stage company should choose the simplest available proxy for value, even an imperfect one, because the discipline of having one number matters more early on than its precision — waiting for a perfect metric is itself a form of procrastination. A larger company, with more data and more teams to coordinate, evolves that single number into an explicit metric tree with owned inputs, as Manzil now needed, because at scale the coordination problem is bigger than the measurement problem.

7. Common Mistakes

Choosing a vanity metric because it is easy to move. Symptom: the growth chart looks excellent while renewal or revenue stalls, as happened to Manzil with MAU. Underlying error: mistaking activity for value delivered. Cheapest diagnostic: segment retention by the metric's own quartiles — if the top quartile retains no better than the bottom, the metric is not measuring value.

Choosing a lagging metric because it feels rigorous. Symptom: teams wait until quarter-end to learn whether the strategy worked, too late to adjust. Underlying error: conflating the outcome the business wants with what a team can influence this month. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether one product decision made this week could move the number within thirty days; if not, it belongs downstream of the North Star.

Optimising the metric without a guardrail. Symptom: the North Star rises steadily while complaints or refunds rise alongside it. Underlying error: treating the definition as bulletproof rather than as something a team under pressure will eventually satisfy literally, not in spirit. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether a documented counter-metric is reviewed in the same meeting, not a separate one weeks later.

Picking the number by committee, without an input tree. Symptom: everyone agrees on the North Star but no team can say which weekly action it implies for them. Underlying error: stopping short of decomposing it into owned inputs. Cheapest diagnostic: ask each pod lead to name, unprompted, the one input metric their team owns; silence is the tell.

8. What Good Looks Like

Six weeks later, Ritika returned with Verified Skill Completions per Active Learner per Month as Manzil's FY27 North Star, alongside a one-page input tree: Pune owned activation rate (starts a module within 48 hours); Hyderabad owned completion-and-pass rate; Gurugram owned the guardrail — quality complaints per hundred completions, reviewed in the same Monday meeting, not a separate one. Each owner had a weekly number, a named decision it fed, and a shared understanding that a rising North Star with a rising complaint rate was not a win. The chairperson's response was relief, not enthusiasm: for the first time in a year, three cities were arguing about the same number for the same reason.

9. What Ritika Decided, and What to Learn Next

Ritika chose Verified Skill Completions over both Monthly Active Users and Employer Placements — not the most impressive-sounding number, but the only candidate that was simultaneously a leading indicator her teams could move within a sprint, a strict-enough proxy for what learners and employers both valued, and decomposable into inputs three cities could each own without stepping on each other. She kept placements as a slower validation metric one layer downstream, not the North Star itself — a distinction the board resisted, since placements sounded like the "real" outcome, until the renewal arithmetic in Figure 2 made the timing problem concrete.

The natural next topic is the metric tree itself — how breadth, depth, and frequency combine into a North Star for products where usage, not a pass/fail assessment, is the unit of value, and how OKRs translate a North Star and its inputs into commitments teams can be held to. Two questions worth sitting with: if your product's most-reported metric went to zero overnight, would customers notice a loss of value, or only your dashboard — and who, by name, owns the number your organisation calls its most important one?

Dhara Agritech: Ten Million Acres

A Pune agritech company has built four businesses, three contracts and one funding round on a single number that its own data scientist now believes is 27 per cent wrong.

1. Sunday night, Aundh

At 11.40 p.m. on Sunday, 8 March 2026, Rukmini Iyer was sitting on the floor of her flat in Aundh, Pune, with her laptop on a low table and the remains of Holi colour still faintly pink along her hairline. On the screen were two documents. The first was the board pre-read for the strategy session that began at nine the next morning, twenty-two pages, of which page four carried the headline Dhara Agritech had used for five years: 9.1 million acres under advisory. The second was a spreadsheet Tanvi Deshpande had sent from Toronto at 6.12 p.m. India time with the subject line "please read before you send the pre-read," which estimated that the true figure, after removing duplicate plots, lapsed leases and households registered more than once, was somewhere between 6.4 and 7.1 million acres.

Rukmini had been chief product officer for three years. She had spent most of the past eleven days trying to work out whether Tanvi's number was a data-quality problem, a metric problem, or a strategy problem wearing the costume of a metric problem. She had not decided. The board would ask her, at some point on Monday, what single number Dhara should run on for FY27, and the four honest answers she could construct each broke something the company had already promised somebody.

2. How Dhara got here, and the decision that still binds it

Dhara Agritech was founded in 2017 by Vivek Salunkhe and Dr Anand Kulkarni, an agronomist who had spent fourteen years at a state agricultural university in Parbhani. Its first product was a free advisory app, Dhara Kisan, delivering sowing windows, pest alerts and nutrition schedules in nine languages. By March 2026 it had 6.8 million registered farmers, of whom 1.9 million had opened the app in February, and it stood in a crowded field: Mahindra's Krish-e, DeHaat, AgroStar and BigHaat all pursued versions of the same farmer, Reliance Retail's sourcing arm was building direct relationships with growers, and IFFCO's own digital initiatives reached villages Dhara's field officers had never visited.

The company had since grown three more limbs. Dhara Bazaar sold seed, crop protection and nutrition products through 4,200 partner retailers, with GMV of ₹1,140 crore in FY26. Dhara Sense leased soil-moisture and micro-weather nodes to farmer producer organisations and large farms — 18,000 nodes deployed. And Dhara Insights sold anonymised, district-level crop-acreage and pest-incidence data to input manufacturers and crop insurers, including a three-year contract with Merevale Crop Science, a US-listed crop-science major, negotiated out of New Jersey.

The decision that constrained everything on Rukmini's Sunday night had been taken in October 2021. To win its first large data contract, Dhara had needed a coverage number quickly, and had defined "acres under advisory" as the sum of self-declared plot areas entered by farmers at onboarding, with no verification and no expiry. The alternative on the table at the time — geo-fenced plot boundaries captured by field officers, with annual re-confirmation — would have taken nine months and about ₹14 crore that the company did not then have. The self-declared definition shipped in five weeks. It went into the data contract, into the NABARD-linked grant agreement of 2023, into three investor decks, and into the FY27 Series D term sheet that sat, unsigned, in Vivek's inbox.

3. The industry around it

Indian agritech in 2026 was being reshaped by three forces that bore directly on Dhara's choice. The first was ONDC, which had begun to commoditise the retail layer of agri-input distribution; a farmer in Nashik could increasingly compare seed prices across sellers without being on any particular platform, which pressed Dhara Bazaar's take rate down from 9.1 per cent in FY24 to 6.8 per cent in FY26. The second was regulatory: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent architecture, whose operative rules had begun to bite, meant that plot-level geo-coordinates linked to an identifiable farmer required fresh, purpose-specific consent, which Dhara did not hold for the 4.1 million plots registered before 2024. Legal counsel in Mumbai had advised that re-consent be completed by November 2026 or the plot-level data be dissociated from farmer identity, which would break the personalised advisory feature that distinguished the product.

The third force was global. Merevale bought Dhara Insights because Indian acreage and pest data was hard to obtain at scale, and priced the contract on coverage. Separately, Al Barsha Fresh Produce, a Dubai importer of Indian grapes and pomegranates, had run a traceability pilot with Dhara in which 620 farmers' consignments were tracked from plot to container, and had indicated interest in scaling to 5,000 farmers at a premium of roughly ₹4.10 per kilogram — a revenue line that depended not on acres or app opens but on verified, plot-level provenance for a small number of export-grade growers.

Meanwhile the macro picture cut across all of it. The 2025 south-west monsoon had been 106 per cent of the long-period average, which had been good for kharif sowing and therefore good for every engagement number Dhara reported; the rabi season had been dry in Marathwada, and February's advisory opens were down 14 per cent year on year in that region while up 9 per cent nationally.

4. The situation in detail

The sequence that brought Rukmini to Sunday night is worth setting out in order, because what was believed at each point mattered as much as what was true.

October 2021. Acres under advisory defined as self-declared, unverified, non-expiring. Believed at the time: verification could be retrofitted later, and self-declaration would be roughly accurate because farmers had no incentive to lie. Now known to be wrong in three ways: a farmer who leased in land for one kharif season kept the acreage forever; households where a father and two sons each installed the app registered overlapping plots; and a 2023 field-officer incentive of ₹40 per registered acre produced a measurable spike in declared plot sizes in exactly the districts where that incentive ran.

July 2024. Dhara signed a handset-bundle distribution arrangement under which Dhara Kisan came pre-installed on a low-cost smartphone sold through rural retail. Believed at the time: this would accelerate genuine reach. Now known: approximately 900,000 of the app's registered farmers arrived this way, and their advisory-open rate in month three was 11 per cent against 38 per cent for organically acquired farmers — but they are indistinguishable from organic users in the monthly active number that appears in the board pack, because the install-source field was not populated for the first five months of the arrangement.

September 2025. Rajesh Pillai closed a renewal discussion with Merevale in which, at Merevale's insistence, the FY27 pricing schedule tied ₹46 crore of annual fees to "verified acres under active advisory," a term the contract defined as plots with a geo-boundary and at least one advisory delivered and opened in the preceding 90 days. Believed at the time: Dhara's 9.1 million acres would comfortably clear the 7.5-million threshold. What has since emerged: on the contract's own definition, Dhara could evidence 3.9 million acres in February 2026.

January 2026. Tanvi's deduplication model, built in Toronto over six weeks, produced the 6.4–7.1 million range. It was validated by ground-truthing in three districts — Nashik, Belagavi and Guntur — where field officers physically visited 1,100 registered plots.

February 2026. The Series D term sheet arrived: ₹340 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹2,900 crore, with a milestone tranche of ₹120 crore released on reaching 10 million acres under advisory by 31 March 2027, "measured on the company's existing published methodology."

5. The people

Incentive: his founder stake and the milestone tranche. Not saying: he has already told two of the incoming investors, informally, that 10 million acres is "conservative."

Meghna Rao, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Position: acres are not revenue and never have been; the company should run on Bazaar contribution margin, which is the only line that can reach break-even within the runway. Incentive: she owns the burn number and has to raise the next round if this one shrinks. Not saying: she has modelled a scenario in which Sense and the Dubai traceability programme are shut down entirely, and it is the only scenario that reaches break-even in 20 months.

Dr Anand Kulkarni, co-founder and chief agronomist, Hyderabad. Position: the only number worth having is yield uplift per acre, because it is the only one a farmer's family would recognise as value; everything else is a proxy for a proxy. Incentive: professional identity and the field-trial programme he runs. Not saying: two of his six district trials lacked proper control groups, and he knows a statistician would not accept the aggregate figure he quotes.

Incentive: delivery credibility; his performance review is tied to shipped roadmap items. Not saying: two services already compute "active advisory" differently — one on delivery, one on open — and the board pack has been using whichever was higher.

Incentive: her team's influence over the roadmap. Not saying: her qualitative sample of 84 farmers was drawn overwhelmingly from Maharashtra and Karnataka smartphone owners with 4G, and the confirmation tap she proposes has a 62 per cent completion rate in usability testing.

Tanvi Deshpande, senior data scientist, Toronto. Position: no metric decision should be taken until the acreage base is deduplicated, and the company should publish the restated series itself rather than have an auditor find it. Incentive: analytical credibility; she is also being recruited by a Canadian insurer. Not saying: her model's confidence interval is wide because ground truth exists for only three districts, and the district where it flags the largest inflation is Parbhani, the programme Vivek personally launched.

Rajesh Pillai, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. Position: whatever the North Star is, it must be the contract definition — verified acres under active advisory — because that is the number that pays ₹46 crore a year, 22 per cent of revenue. Incentive: his commission is on Insights renewals. Not saying: he believes Merevale inserted the verified-acre clause because their own analysts had already noticed inconsistencies in Dhara's district files.

Nadia Haq, customer-success lead, Singapore, who manages the Al Barsha relationship from a time zone that overlaps both Dubai and Bengaluru. Position: the export traceability programme is the highest-value-per-farmer thing Dhara does and is invisible in every metric the company reports; the North Star should be traceable tonnage. Incentive: her programme's survival. Not saying: Al Barsha's commitment is a letter of intent, not a contract, and their procurement head has asked twice about Dhara's ability to guarantee volumes during a dry rabi.

8. The options as Rukmini sees them

Option A — hold the line, verify quietly. Keep acres under advisory on the existing published methodology, sign the Series D, and run a verification programme through FY27 so that the reported and deduplicated figures converge by FY28. Upside: nothing breaks this quarter, and the milestone tranche stays reachable. Cost: the Merevale renewal still has to be met on a definition Dhara currently fails by 3.6 million acres, and every month of delay increases the chance that the restatement is discovered rather than disclosed.

Option B — adopt the contract definition. Make verified acres under active advisory the North Star, aligning the company with the revenue line that pays best. Upside: auditable, externally validated, and it forces the geo-boundary and re-consent work the DPDP timeline requires anyway. Cost: the headline number falls from 9.1 million to 3.9 million; the term-sheet milestone becomes unreachable on any reading; and, as Exhibit 5 shows, the metric rises with field-officer paperwork rather than farmer behaviour.

Option C — adopt a behavioural metric. Monthly farmers who act on an advisory, as Lea proposes, or advisories acted upon per active farmer. Upside: measures something a farmer does, decomposes into reach, relevance and confirmation, and is movable by the product team. Cost: it requires the taxonomy work Hardik says trades against the Bazaar revamp; the confirmation signal is self-reported and completes 62 per cent of the time; it says nothing about Insights, Sense or the export programme; and it collapses in the off-season, which in a two-season crop calendar is half the year.

Option D — adopt contribution margin, as Meghna wants. Upside: it is the only number tied to survival, and the runway is 14 months. Cost: it is a lagging outcome, it would direct the entire company towards Bazaar's large-farmer GMV as shown in Exhibit 6, and it puts Dhara in a take-rate race against ONDC-enabled sellers that it has been losing for two years.

Rukmini had written all four on a page and then, at around eleven, written a fifth line beneath them and not crossed it out: are we one company? The four options assumed a single scoreboard was the right artefact. But Insights sells coverage, Bazaar sells transactions, Sense sells uptime, and the Dubai programme sells provenance for 620 farmers at a premium per kilogram — and it was not obvious that the same number could carry all four, or that the board's question was really about measurement rather than about which of the four businesses Dhara intended to be.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board strategy session opened at 9 a.m. on Monday, 9 March 2026, and Vivek wanted a metric recommendation before lunch, because the Series D signing window closed on 27 March. The binding constraints were these. Cash: ₹252 crore on hand, burn ₹18 crore a month, 14 months of runway; the milestone tranche of ₹120 crore was tied to 10 million acres by 31 March 2027 on the existing methodology. Contracts: the Merevale schedule tied ₹46 crore a year — 22 per cent of revenue, 38 per cent of contribution margin — to a definition Dhara met at 3.9 million against a 7.5-million threshold, with the FY27 pricing effective 1 July 2026. Grants: ₹12 crore of NABARD-linked disbursement reported against acreage, with the next report due in June 2026. Regulation: DPDP consent re-collection for 4.1 million pre-2024 plots by November 2026, or dissociation of plot data from farmer identity. People: a headcount freeze, and Hardik's 31 engineers able to deliver instrumentation rework or the Bazaar checkout revamp, not both; Tanvi had a competing offer in Toronto. And one soft constraint that Rukmini suspected mattered most: Dr Kulkarni and Vivek had founded the company together, and neither had ever lost an argument about what Dhara was for.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What exactly does "9.1 million acres under advisory" measure? Write the definition as an arithmetic expression, then list every way the number can rise without any farmer receiving more value.

2. Exhibits 2, 3 and 5 give three different pictures of the same nine months. Which of them, if any, would you put in front of the board, and what would you say about the ones you leave out?

3. Dr Kulkarni argues that yield uplift is the only measure a farmer's family would recognise. Using Exhibit 4, state the strongest case for his position and the strongest case against it. What would it take to make yield uplift measurable at the cadence a company needs?

4. Exhibit 6 suggests that Dhara's commercial gravity and its stated mission point at different farmers. If a North Star must express the vision in a number, which vision is Dhara's current metric expressing?

5. Rukmini's fifth line asks whether Dhara is one company. If the answer is no, what would a two-level metric structure look like, what would sit at the top, and what would the board lose by accepting it?

6. What should Rukmini do on Monday morning, in what order, and in what words — and what exactly should she say to the board about the difference between 9.1 and 6.57, given that the term sheet, the Merevale schedule and the NABARD report all rest on the larger figure?

11. Aundh, 1.20 a.m.

Rukmini had drafted three versions of page four. The first kept 9.1 million and added a footnote about an ongoing verification programme. The second showed 9.1 million and 6.57 million side by side with Tanvi's interval, under a heading she kept rewriting. The third dropped acreage from page four altogether and opened with 412,000 buying farmers and ₹10 crore of contribution margin, which was honest, small, and would read to the board as a surrender.

Her phone showed a message from Nadia in Singapore, sent forty minutes earlier: Al Barsha's procurement head wanted a call on Tuesday about the grape window. Beneath it, unanswered, was Tanvi's question from Toronto — whether to include the Parbhani district breakdown in the appendix. Outside, a late Holi speaker was still going somewhere near the canal. Rukmini closed the laptop, then opened it again, and made no change to page four.

Bachat Money: One Number for FY27

A fast-growing Indian savings app has three plausible candidates for its North Star metric, and the choice will decide where ₹64 crore of next year's spending goes.

1. Sankranti weekend

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 January 2026, while most of Bengaluru was on holiday for Sankranti, Sneha Kulkarni was in the empty fourth-floor office of Bachat Money on Bannerghatta Road with two printouts and a cold filter coffee. As director of product, she had been asked by the chief executive, Kartik Menon, to bring one recommendation to the board's annual planning meeting on 31 January: the single metric on which Bachat Money would be judged in FY27, and the one on which the product organisation's goals, the marketing budget and the quarterly bonus pool would all be hung.

Kartik's brief had been short. "Last year we ran on monthly transacting users because that is what the Series C deck said. It has taken us to numbers I am not sure I believe. Give me a number I can defend to the board for three years, and tell me what it will cost us to switch."

2. Bachat Money

Bachat Money was founded in Pune in 2019 and moved to Bengaluru in 2021. Its proposition was small, frequent saving for salaried and self-employed Indians who had never held a demat account: ₹10 a day into digital gold, recurring deposits with partner banks, and, since 2023, mutual funds distributed as a SEBI-registered investment adviser's referral partner. Collections ran on UPI Autopay, which NPCI's mandate rails had made cheap and reliable, and the app's defining feature was a "streak" — an unbroken run of daily or weekly contributions, borrowed shamelessly from language-learning apps.

By December 2025 the company had 18.4 million registered users, 2.6 million monthly transacting users, and assets under management of ₹4,830 crore. Revenue for FY26 was tracking to ₹211 crore, roughly 62 per cent from gold spreads and distribution commissions and the rest from a ₹99-a-month premium tier. Around it stood Groww and Zerodha's Coin for mutual funds, Paytm Money and PhonePe for gold, and a cluster of habit-savings apps for the ₹10-a-day segment. Bachat Money's differentiation was neither product breadth nor price; it was that people who started a streak tended to keep it.

One corridor mattered disproportionately. Since 2024, Bachat Money had run an NRI product for Indians working in the Gulf, distributed through employers, and its largest partner was Al Noor Facilities Management in Dubai, whose 11,400 blue-collar employees could route a fixed share of wages into gold or recurring deposits before the money reached their local accounts. The corridor was 4 per cent of users and 19 per cent of AUM.

3. The situation

Monthly transacting users had been a good servant and had become a poor master. Through 2025 the number had risen 41 per cent, helped by a Diwali campaign offering ₹51 of free gold for a first purchase and by a referral scheme. But in November, Farida Qureshi, Bachat Money's data scientist in Toronto, had circulated an analysis that Sneha could not unsee. Of the members who first transacted between January and March 2025, 38 per cent had made exactly one contribution and never returned; a further 21 per cent had withdrawn their entire balance within 90 days. The cohort's contribution to AUM twelve months on was ₹41 per acquired member against a blended acquisition cost of ₹186.

Farida's second finding was the more useful one. Members who reached a 90-day unbroken streak — contributing at least once in each of thirteen consecutive weeks — behaved differently in every respect that mattered. They were 4.6 times more likely to be active a year later, held 11 times the average balance, and were the only segment from which the ₹99 premium tier sold at all.

The global team read the same numbers differently, as teams in different time zones do. Ravi Deshmukh, the engineering lead in Pune, wanted whatever number required least new instrumentation; streaks were computed nightly in a batch job he did not trust and could not easily make real-time. Ananya Sen, the design lead in Berlin, argued that streaks were the only part of the product users spoke about unprompted in research, and that measuring them would finally align the roadmap with the thing customers valued. Arjun Rao, head of NRI partnerships in New Jersey, pointed out that the Gulf corridor's members saved through payroll deduction and therefore could not break a streak even if they wanted to, so a streak metric would flatter his segment and tell him nothing. Nisha Pillai, customer-success lead in Singapore who handled the Al Noor relationship, added that Al Noor's human-resources head judged the programme by rupees accumulated per worker, not by behaviour.

4. The people

Kartik Menon, chief executive, Bengaluru, wanted a number the board would accept for three years and that would not look like a retreat from growth. He had told investors the company would cross 4 million monthly transacting users in FY27. Farida Qureshi, data scientist, Toronto, wanted the metric that best predicted AUM twelve months out, and was indifferent to how hard it was to compute. Priya Balakrishnan, vice-president of growth, Bengaluru, held a ₹64 crore FY27 marketing budget whose performance was measured in cost per transacting user; a switch to a retention-shaped metric would make half her channels look unprofitable overnight. Arjun Rao, NRI partnerships, New Jersey, wanted AUM, because AUM was the language his employer partners in Dubai and Sharjah spoke, and because his commission plan was built on it.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the spine of the case. The bottom row is 12 per cent of the cohort and, by the twelfth month, holds roughly 88 per cent of the cohort's balances. The top two rows together are 59 per cent of the cohort, contributed almost all of the reported growth in monthly transacting users, and are worth nothing. Any metric that treats those two groups as equivalent to the fourth row is measuring the company's marketing activity rather than its customers' saving.

AUM is sensitive to the gold price, which rose 23 per cent during FY26; the data team estimated that ₹640 crore of the ₹4,830 crore was price appreciation rather than net inflow.

Exhibit 2 sharpens the trade-off. AUM is the number the board and Al Noor understand, but it is the outcome rather than the lever, and roughly one rupee in seven of last year's growth came from the gold price rather than from anything Bachat Money did. Monthly transacting users is the only candidate any single team can move on demand, which is precisely why it was chosen in FY26 and precisely why it drifted.

Exhibit 3 is the picture Kartik had not seen. The two bars tell opposite stories about the same year, and the fourth-quarter divergence — transacting users up, streaks down — is the clearest available evidence that FY26's chosen number had stopped carrying information about the health of the business.

6. The options

Option A: keep monthly transacting users. The advantages are real and should not be dismissed. The number is already instrumented, already in the board pack, already in Priya's channel-level reporting, and already promised to investors at 4 million for FY27. Growth can move it predictably. The cost is that Bachat Money would spend another year buying members who are worth ₹41 each at ₹186 each, and would enter FY28 with a larger registered base and no better business.

Option B: adopt assets under management. AUM is what the board, the partner banks, Al Noor's human-resources head and Arjun's commission plan all already speak. It is unambiguous, audited, and cannot be gamed by a free-gold offer. The costs are three. It lags product work by six to twelve months; it moves with the gold price, so a good quarter and a bad quarter can be indistinguishable from a price chart; and no product team can act on it directly, which means it would be decomposed informally by every team in its own way.

Option C: adopt members with a live 90-day savings streak. This measures a customer doing the thing the company exists to help them do, it predicts AUM and premium conversion strongly, and it decomposes cleanly into new streaks started, streaks sustained and streaks recovered — three levers with three plausible owners. The costs are equally concrete: the number is a tenth the size of the one investors have been shown, it is computed in a batch job Ravi does not trust, it structurally flatters the payroll-deduction corridor, and it would immediately reprice half of Priya's marketing channels.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, what did FY26's 41 per cent growth in monthly transacting users actually buy Bachat Money? State the answer in rupees per acquired member.

2. Which of the three candidates in Exhibit 2 measures value received by the customer, which measures value received by the company, and which measures neither? What follows from that classification?

3. Arjun Rao's Gulf corridor cannot break a streak because contributions are deducted from payroll. Does that make Option C wrong, or does it mean the metric needs a different treatment for that segment — and what would that treatment be?

4. What should Sneha recommend on 31 January, and what exactly should she tell Kartik it will cost in the first two quarters?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an exercise in applying the three tests a North Star metric must pass: it should express value the customer would recognise as having been received, it should lead the business result in time rather than lag it, and it should be decomposable into levers a team can move within a planning cycle. Each option in the case fails or passes these tests in a different, diagnosable way. Monthly transacting users passes the third test and fails the first two — a single ₹10 gold purchase is not value received in any sense a customer would recognise, and Exhibit 1 shows it does not lead revenue. AUM passes the first test partially and fails the other two — it is the lagging result, contaminated by a commodity price that no one in the company controls. Streak-holding members is the only candidate that passes all three, which is what makes the case tractable for a learner even though it is not free of cost.

A well-reasoned answer does three things beyond naming the option. It quantifies the switch, rather than asserting it: 0.71 million against 2.60 million is a tenth of the headline, and someone has to explain that to the board without it reading as a downgrade. It builds the tree, because a North Star without input metrics is a poster — new streaks started, streaks sustained past week thirteen, and streaks recovered after a break, each with a named owner. And it installs guardrails for the specific harms this metric invites: a streak metric rewards nagging, so notification volume per member and complaint rate belong on the guardrail list, as does average contribution size, since a company could multiply streaks by encouraging ₹10 habits that never grow.

One defensible path is therefore to adopt Option C as the North Star while retaining both other numbers in named roles. Sneha recommends members with a live 90-day streak as the FY27 North Star; keeps monthly transacting users as an input metric owned by Priya, reframed as new streaks started so that her channels are judged on the quality of what they bring; keeps AUM as the board-facing business outcome, reported alongside the North Star with the gold-price effect separated out; and asks for Arjun's Gulf corridor to be reported separately, since a payroll-deducted streak is a different behaviour from a voluntary one and averaging them would hide both. Two conditions make this path honest rather than merely tidy: Ravi's batch job must be hardened and the definition version-numbered before the metric carries a bonus, and the cohort analysis behind Exhibit 1 must be re-run in November 2026 to confirm that streaks still predict AUM after a year of the company deliberately trying to manufacture them.

The test of a North Star is not whether it is flattering but whether the company would change course if it fell. On that test, Bachat Money's FY26 number had already failed.
